summary.text: 1816 is called the Year Without a Summer because severe climate abnormalities lowered average global temperatures by 0.4–0.7 °C.
The main cause is generally held to be a volcanic winter from Mount Tambora's April 1815 eruption, whose ash and gases blocked sunlight and cooled the globe.
Crops failed and food ran short across the Northern Hemisphere, and Europe's food riots of 1816 and 1817 were its most violent since the French Revolution.

facts.label: Eruption size
facts.value: VEI 7, at least 37 km³ of material ejected

facts.label: Hardest hit
facts.value: New England, Atlantic Canada and Western Europe

facts.value: The last great subsistence crisis in the Western world

items.prompt: A volcano erupted in Indonesia in April 1815, and the next summer brought frost to New England. How could a faraway eruption chill summers across the globe?

options.label: Lava flows warmed the ocean and shifted currents
The blast's shock wave pushed polar air south
Ash and gases in the air blocked sunlight
Earthquakes from the blast tilted the Earth

items.explain: Ash, gases and dust thrown high into the atmosphere blocked sunlight in the stratosphere, so temperatures fell worldwide.

items.prompt: After crops failed in New England in 1816, many farm families left their homes looking for better land. What larger trend in the United States did this feed?
items.explain: Families went in search of better farming opportunities, which contributed to westward expansion.

items.prompt: In 1816 India's summer monsoon arrived late and then brought torrential rains. Which disease did this help spread from Bengal all the way to Moscow?
items.explain: The late, heavy rains aggravated the spread of cholera from a region near the Ganges in Bengal as far as Moscow.

items.prompt: When the cold summer of 1816 hit, Europe was already in a weak position to cope with failed harvests. What had worn it down?

options.label: A fresh outbreak of the Black Death

items.explain: Europe was still recovering from the Napoleonic Wars, which added to the stress of the food shortages.

items.prompt: Tambora erupted near the end of the Little Ice Age, a cooling period that had lasted for centuries. How did that timing shape 1816?

options.label: The eruption ended the cold period
It added to cooling already under way

items.explain: Earth was already in a long cooling period, and the eruption made that background cooling worse.

items.prompt: May 1816 had the lowest Wolf number on record, during a stretch of low solar activity. What does this tell us about the sun's role in the cold?

options.label: The weak sun was the main cause
The overlap alone proves no link
Low solar activity explains it all
The quiet sun warmed Earth instead

items.explain: It is not yet known whether solar changes affect climate, and this overlap does not prove low solar activity causes cooling.

paragraphs.heading: A year that lost its warmth
paragraphs.text: People call 1816 the Year Without a Summer. That year the climate went badly wrong, and the average temperature of the whole planet dropped by 0.4–0.7 °C. In Europe, the summer was colder than any other recorded between 1766 and 2000. Harvests failed and food ran short across the Northern Hemisphere. The hardest-hit places were New England, Atlantic Canada and Western Europe.

paragraphs.heading: A volcano on the other side of the world
paragraphs.text: The chief cause is generally thought to be a volcanic winter, a spell of cooling brought on by a huge eruption. In April 1815, Mount Tambora erupted on the island of Sumbawa, in what is now Indonesia. It scored 7 on the volcanic explosivity index (VEI), a scale of how big an eruption is, and threw out at least 37 km³ of dense-rock equivalent material. No later eruption has been confirmed at VEI 7. Ash and gases spread through the atmosphere, blocked sunlight in the stratosphere, and the world cooled.

paragraphs.heading: Other things piling on
paragraphs.text: Tambora did not act alone. An 1814 eruption of Mayon in the Philippines may have made its effect worse, and smaller drops in temperature followed eruptions in 1812–1814. Earth was also near the end of the Little Ice Age, a cooling that had lasted since the 14th century and had already hurt farming in Europe. The Sun was quiet too, in a stretch of low activity called the Dalton Minimum, though it is still unknown whether that affects Earth's climate.

paragraphs.heading: Hunger and riots in Europe
paragraphs.text: Europe had not yet recovered from the Napoleonic Wars when the cold arrived. Cold weather and heavy rain ruined harvests in Great Britain and Ireland, and in Ireland the wheat, oat and potato crops all failed. Food prices climbed sharply across the continent, and the century's worst famine followed. With no one knowing the cause, hungry crowds gathered outside grain markets and bakeries. No period on the continent since the French Revolution had seen riots as violent as those of 1816 and 1817.

paragraphs.heading: Frost in an American summer
paragraphs.text: In the eastern United States, a lasting "dry fog" dimmed the Sun and brought cold and frost all through the summer months. Crops failed in places such as New England, and people went hungry and lost money. Many families left their homes to look for better farmland, which helped push settlement westward. Historian John D. Post described 1816 as the Western world's last great subsistence crisis.

paragraphs.heading: Effects across Asia and Africa
paragraphs.text: The disruption reached far beyond Europe and America. In China the monsoon was upset, the Yangtze Valley flooded, and snow fell in summer in parts of Jiangxi and Anhui. A great famine in Yunnan helped turn the fortunes of the ruling Qing dynasty. In India, a late monsoon brought heavy rains that helped cholera spread from Bengal as far as Moscow. Off South Africa, a violent storm near Cape Town in July 1816 badly damaged ships.
